rules.quote: Complete a sentence with a full stop
rules.violation_condition: A completed sentence that is neither a question nor an exclamation lacks its final full stop, outside the stated exceptions.
when: Applies to sentences that are not questions or exclamations.
A list of sentence fragments completing a sentence takes the final full stop after its last item.
The fragment-list requirement does not apply to stand-alone lists with a heading without a colon.
Sentences ending in link text still require a final full stop, outside the link.
In government social media, a full stop is not required when the post ends in a URL, a tag or handle, a hashtag, an emoji or a sentence fragment.
Government text messages take a final full stop when they finish with a sentence, but not when they finish with a fragment or sign off.
The page separately excludes full stops from headings, stand-alone lists, page headers or footers, captions and titles.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: sentence-fragment lists, linked sentence endings and SMS sentences are cases or restatements of the sentence-ending check; G-3: social-media permissions limit it.

examples.note: The inline example illustrates the required decimal separator.

rules.quote: as the decimal point in numbers and currency
rules.violation_condition: A decimal number or currency amount uses a separator other than a full stop between its integer and fractional parts.
when: Applies when a number or currency amount is written with a decimal fractional part.
rules.why: G-1: decimal notation is a distinct check under the heading grouping numbers and shortened forms.

examples.note: The inline example shows a full stop between numbering components.

rules.quote: in numbering subsections and paragraphs in a document
rules.specification: Read this as requiring full stops between components of hierarchical numbering, as illustrated by ‘Section 7.3’, rather than a trailing full stop after every section or paragraph identifier.
rules.violation_condition: A multi-part subsection or paragraph number lacks full stops between its numbering components.
when: Applies when subsections or paragraphs use multi-part hierarchical numbering.
rules.why: G-1: document numbering is separate from decimal notation and shortened forms; E-4: the interpretation of the numbering scope is explicit.

rules.quote: in some Latin shortened forms and shortened forms used in referencing.
rules.specification: The page does not identify which shortened forms require full stops or their exact punctuation. A list of prescribed forms is needed before this check can be implemented.
rules.violation_condition: A Latin shortened form or referencing shortened form that requires full stops is written without them.
when: Applies only to shortened forms conventionally written with full stops, not to all Latin shortened forms or all referencing shortened forms.
rules.why: G-1 and G-2: one required-punctuation check covers the specified subset of shortened forms without extending it to every form.

rules.quote: Don’t use full stops with contractions or most abbreviations.
rules.specification: The page does not enumerate the exceptions to ‘most abbreviations’. Checking requires a list distinguishing forms that take full stops from those that do not.
rules.violation_condition: A contraction or abbreviation contains a full stop even though its prescribed form does not take one.
when: Applies to contractions and abbreviations that do not conventionally take full stops.
Some Latin shortened forms and shortened forms used in referencing are exceptions.
rules.why: G-2: contractions and abbreviations share the prohibited-full-stop check, with the exceptions retained rather than treated as a blanket ban.

when: The address is part of a sentence fragment or is on a line by itself.
This does not prohibit the full stops within the address.
rules.why: G-4: the body supplies the scope missing from the heading; G-2: fragment and stand-alone-line contexts are cases of one check.

Concerns full stops within the address, not punctuation added after it.
rules.why: G-4: the prose after the example states a separate rule about address spelling, not terminal sentence punctuation.
